analysis.one_liner: Bans new mining claims on a million acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 236-185 to bar new mining on about 1,006,545 acres near the Grand Canyon, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently take roughly 1,006,545 acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon off the table for new mining claims, including uranium mining under the 1872 mining law, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing. Its stated purpose is to protect the canyon's watershed, ecosystem, and cultural heritage for current and future generations. Existing mining rights would be grandfathered in. The House passed it 236-185, but it died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The people whose drinking water comes from the Colorado River and its tributaries, which rise near and flow through the withdrawn lands, gain protection from the contamination risk of new uranium mining in the Grand Canyon watershed. Tribes in the region whose lands and sacred sites surround the canyon, and the recreation and tourism economy built on the canyon, also gain from a permanently protected landscape. Future generations gain because the withdrawal is permanent rather than subject to periodic administrative renewal.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Colorado River water users and canyon-area tribes

how_it_helps.text: Permanently withdraws approximately 1,006,545 acres of federal land in Arizona from new mining claims under the mining laws and from mineral and geothermal leasing, locking in protection rather than leaving the area open to claim-staking.

States its purpose as protecting, for current and future generations, the watershed, ecosystem, and cultural heritage of the Grand Canyon region — the watershed drains toward the Colorado River, the water source for millions downstream.
Honors valid existing rights, so it targets future mining activity rather than seizing anything anyone already lawfully holds.
Survived a full committee review and a floor vote, winning a 236-185 House majority, including 9 of 197 Republicans — showing broad, though not bipartisan, support.

analysis.who_pays: Uranium and other mining companies lose the ability to stake new claims, explore, and develop mineral deposits across the roughly one million acres. Supporters of the region's small uranium industry argued its jobs and America's domestic uranium supply bear the cost, pointing to reliance on imported uranium from countries like Russia and Kazakhstan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Uranium mining companies near the canyon

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal is subject to valid existing rights, so companies with claims already staked before enactment could keep developing them; the bill stops new mining but does not shut down mines already in the pipeline.

Opponents argued that closing the area to domestic mining would increase U.S. reliance on imported uranium from countries like Russia, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Namibia — a real national-supply tradeoff the bill does not address.

The cost falls on the small uranium mining industry and mining-dependent communities in northern Arizona, which lose their main prospective ore body near the canyon; the bill offers those workers and towns nothing in return.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — permanent protection of the Grand Canyon watershed and the Colorado River's headwaters from new uranium mining — is large and durable, and the bill carefully leaves valid existing rights untouched. The cost is real but narrow: a small uranium industry loses access to prospective deposits, and the country gives up domestic production from this specific area, which opponents said means more foreign uranium. Weighing a small industry's ore body against the water supply of a major river, the tradeoff favors protection, though the foreign-supply concern is a fair objection the bill does not answer.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 236-185, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on February 26, 2019, to withdraw about 1,006,545 acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon from new mining claims.
The House Natural Resources Committee, which Grijalva chaired, reported the bill amended on October 4, 2019, after a 21-14 committee vote, and it was placed on the calendar for a floor vote.

Republicans tried to weaken or slow it on the floor: Rep. Paul Gosar offered three amendments, all of which failed, and Rep. Rob Wittman's motion to send the bill back with instructions to first study whether the withdrawal would increase uranium imports from Russia and other countries failed 196-226.
On October 30, 2019, the House passed the bill 236-185, with 227 of 233 Democrats and 9 of 197 Republicans voting yes.
The Senate received the bill the next day and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which took no further action; the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Uranium mining interests came out ahead: the land around the Grand Canyon stayed open to new claims and leasing, and no Senate action forced a reckoning with the issue.

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.role: House sponsor; Chair, Committee on Natural Resources
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, steered it through committee markup (21-14) to a floor vote, and managed the debate as a pattern of motions on the floor show.

for.name: 122 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, and 227 House Democrats ultimately voted for it on passage.

for.name: Havasupai Tribe and Grand Canyon-area tribes
for.role: Tribal nations whose lands and water surround the withdrawn area
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed protection of the Grand Canyon watershed from uranium mining, the concern the bill's purpose clause addresses.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 31, 2019, referred it to itself, and never held a markup or vote; the bill expired there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the remainder of the 116th Congress.

against.name: 183 of 197 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans voting no on passage
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage 236-185, keeping the bill from anything resembling bipartisan support.

against.name: Paul Gosar
against.what_they_did: Offered three amendments on the floor to change the bill; all were rejected.

against.name: Rob Wittman
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions requiring a study of whether the withdrawal would increase uranium imports from Russia and other countries; failed 196-226.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost entirely by party: 227 of 233 Democrats voted yes while only 9 of 197 Republicans did, and the losing motion to recommit drew 193 of 197 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill closes about a million acres of the Grand Canyon watershed — the heart of Arizona's remaining high-grade uranium deposits — to new claims and development, though existing rights are grandfathered. The industry's profits depend on mining land that drains toward the Colorado River, the water supply for millions, which is exactly what the bill stops.

industries.industry: Grand Canyon tourism and outdoor recreation
industries.note: A permanent mining ban protects the landscape, watershed, and ecosystem the canyon's recreation economy depends on, and it removes the uncertainty of periodic temporary withdrawals.
Opponents argued that withdrawing domestic uranium lands pushes U.S. buyers toward imported uranium from countries like Russia and Kazakhstan; the bill does not address supply or substitution.
